intro: Four modules cover the two services nearly every network depends on: how DNS resolves names and which record types matter, how to troubleshoot it, how DHCP hands out addresses with scopes, leases and relays, and the everyday problems you will fix. Practice in the labs, including simulated DNS and DHCP consoles.

sources.title: Cloudflare Learning Center: What is DNS?

modules.title: How DNS works
modules.summary: Follow a name lookup from your PC to the answer, and learn the record types you will manage.

blocks.p: The Domain Name System turns names people remember (www.example.com) into IP addresses computers use. Without it nothing on the internet or in an office network would be reachable by name. DNS is a distributed, hierarchical database: the root, then top-level domains (.com), then domains (example.com), then hosts.

head: Part
Role
rows: Asks the configured DNS server and caches answers
Does the searching for the client, caches results (your ISP, or your office DNS server)
Holds the real records for a zone and gives the official answer

steps.d: Your PC checks its cache and the hosts file.
It sends the query to its configured DNS server.
If not cached, the resolver asks a root server, then the .com servers, then the domain's authoritative server.
The answer returns and is cached for the record's TTL (time to live).

blocks.note: DNS uses UDP port 53 for most queries and TCP port 53 for large responses and zone transfers.

tips: A CNAME must point to a name, never to an IP address.
Lower the TTL before a planned change so old answers expire quickly.
Think of the hosts file as a local override that beats DNS.
terms: A DNS server or client component that looks up names on behalf of others.
Holds the official records for a zone.
The portion of the DNS namespace managed as one unit.
How long an answer may be cached, in seconds.
One entry in a zone, such as an A or MX record.

modules.title: Troubleshooting DNS
modules.summary: Use nslookup, dig and cache commands to separate name problems from network problems.

blocks.p: If you can reach 8.8.8.8 by IP but not www.example.com by name, the network is fine and DNS is the suspect. If neither works, check addressing, gateway and cabling first.

modules.title: How DHCP works
modules.summary: Understand how clients receive addresses automatically, and how scopes, reservations and relays fit in.

blocks.p: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) gives clients an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers and more, so nobody has to type them by hand. Clients use UDP port 68; servers use UDP 67.

steps.d: Client broadcasts: is there a DHCP server?
Client asks to use the offered address.
Server confirms and starts the lease.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The range of addresses a server hands out for one subnet (for example 192.168.10.100 to .200)
How long a client may use an address; it renews at 50% of the lease time
Addresses inside the range the server must not hand out (for static servers and printers)
A fixed address given to a specific MAC address

blocks.p: Broadcasts do not cross routers. A DHCP relay agent (on Cisco, ip helper-address) forwards client requests to a DHCP server on another subnet, so one server can serve many VLANs. If a client gets no answer it assigns itself an APIPA address in 169.254.0.0/16, which cannot reach other networks.

blocks.note: Use reservations for printers and other devices that need a fixed address but are still managed centrally.

tips: 169.254.x.x on a client means DHCP failed.
Keep static servers outside the scope or in an exclusion.
Only authorized DHCP servers should exist on a network; a rogue server hands out bad settings.
terms: Protocol that automatically assigns IP settings.
A pool of addresses for one subnet.
Time a client may keep an address.
A permanent address tied to a MAC address.
Self-assigned 169.254.0.0/16 address used when DHCP fails.

blocks.p: When hosts get new addresses, DNS must follow. Dynamic DNS (DDNS) lets DHCP clients or the DHCP server register records automatically; scavenging removes stale ones. Without it you get records that point to the wrong machine, or names that fail after a rename.

list: Update the A record and the PTR (reverse) record
Use CNAMEs for friendly names (intranet → web01) so only one record changes when the server moves
Lower the TTL before a migration, raise it after

blocks.note: Document static assignments. Undocumented static IPs cause most duplicate-address problems.

Check the DHCP server address in ipconfig /all to spot a rogue server.
After changing records, flush caches before testing.
